h1: Training a new assistant brewer in 30 days
title: Training a New Assistant Brewer | Craft Beer School
desc: A week-by-week 30-day plan to train a new assistant brewer: safety and cleaning, cellar work, brew days, then a supervised brew and sign-off.
teaser: Hand a new hire a hose and hope: you will be cleaning up mistakes for months. Thirty structured days fixes most of it.
standfirst: A new assistant brewer can be useful in a month and safe on day one, if the training has an order. Here is the 30-day plan we use, week by week, with what to sign off before moving on.
sections: Why the first month decides the next year

Most small breweries train by shadowing. The new assistant follows the head brewer around and picks things up. Some things they pick up well. Others they learn wrong and repeat for years, because nobody ever wrote down the right way.

A structured month costs the head brewer some time. It saves far more in spoiled batches, broken equipment and injuries. It also tells you within thirty days whether the hire was right. Your brewhouse SOPs are the backbone of the plan, so write the core ones before the new person arrives.

Prepare a competency checklist: every task the assistant must be able to do alone, with a column for the date trained and a column for the date signed off. Issue boots, gloves, goggles and a face shield. Decide who trains them each day. A new hire who spends the first morning waiting for someone to notice them learns that the job is not taken seriously.

Nothing else until this is done. The first week covers the hazards that hurt people in breweries:

  • Chemicals. Caustic and acid handling, dilution, PPE and what to do after a splash. Show them the eyewash and the safety data sheets.
  • CO2. Fermenting tanks release large volumes of it and it collects in low, closed spaces. Never put a head inside a tank. Know where the CO2 monitor is and what its alarm means.
  • Heat and pressure. Hot liquor, steam, pressurised tanks and why you never open a fitting under pressure.

Then cleaning: the CIP routine, sanitising hoses and fittings, cleaning the floor and drains. Cleaning is most of brewing. It also teaches the layout of every pipe and valve.

Move to the cold side. Daily fermenter checks: temperature, gravity, pressure, smell. Teach them to take a gravity reading properly and correct it for temperature, since a hydrometer calibrated at 20 °C reads wrong on a warm sample. Have them fill in the fermentation log every day.

Add transfers under supervision: purging with CO2, connecting hoses without picking up oxygen, recording volumes. In a brewpub those volumes feed the excise registers, so accuracy matters beyond the beer.

The assistant now works brew days alongside the brewer, a different stage each day. Milling and checking the crush. Mash-in at the right temperature and water to grist ratio. Lautering without compacting the bed. The boil and hop additions. Knockout, cooling, aeration and pitching.

At each stage ask them why, not just what. An assistant who knows why the sparge water must stay below about 78 °C will not raise it to speed things up when the brewer's back is turned.
Week 4: a supervised brew and sign-off

In the last week the assistant runs a full brew, start to finish, with the head brewer watching and only stepping in for safety or a real error. Run a second one if the first was rough. Then go through the competency checklist line by line and sign off what they can do alone. Anything not signed off stays supervised.

Finish with an honest conversation about what went well and what did not. Make a plan for the next sixty days: yeast handling, basic lab work, sensory training.

Expect mistakes during the month and plan for them. Give the assistant low-risk jobs to fail at, like a hose connected the wrong way during a water rinse, rather than a live transfer of finished beer. A mistake caught in training is cheap. The same mistake made alone on a Sunday night is not.

The hard part of this plan is not the assistant. It is the head brewer finding the time and patience to teach while still brewing. If the brewery is newly open or the head brewer is new themselves, an outside trainer for the first two weeks often pays for itself.

Whoever trains, keep the checklist after sign-off. It becomes the template for every later hire and shows inspectors and partners that your team was trained, not just told.
faqs: Can a new assistant brewer be trained in a month?
They can learn to work safely and run the routine tasks in about 30 days with a structured plan. Judgement on recipes, yeast and troubleshooting takes much longer.
What should a new brewery hire learn first?
Safety: chemical handling, CO2 hazards, heat and pressure. Cleaning comes next, because it teaches the layout of the brewery and makes up most of the work.
How do I know the training worked?
Use a competency checklist and sign off each task only when the assistant does it alone, correctly, under observation. Anything not signed off stays supervised.
